chunks: "The main ones are these. Series termination: a resistor at the driver so that driver impedance plus resistor equals Z0.
It uses no DC power and only works with the receiver at the end.

Parallel termination: a resistor equal to Z0 from the end of the line to a reference, ground or a mid-rail VTT; it gives a clean wave along the whole line, but a CMOS driver has to drive that DC load, so power is high.

Thevenin or split termination: two resistors, one to the supply and one to ground, with a parallel value of Z0, so it sets a DC bias at the receiver too, say 100 and 100 ohms for 50 ohms at half the supply.
It still burns DC power. AC termination: Z0 in series with a capacitor, so there's no DC current but the capacitor has to be large enough, around 100 picofarads to a nanofarad.
Differential termination: a resistor across the pair, typically 100 ohms, often on-die.
Then there are diode clamps, Schottky diodes to the rails that don't match but limit overshoot, and DDR's VTT termination and on-die termination.

The choice is topology and power: series for point-to-point where I want low power, parallel or Thevenin for multi-drop or when I need a clean wave all along the line, AC when DC power matters, differential for pairs."
